aliases: Independent Research Programme -- KnowledgeOS as the Brain of a Computer
note: A commissioned third, independent research-programme prompt (explicitly not to read or depend on Session 1/Session 2 conclusions) organizing 17 questions (Q0 what would a computer brain need, through Q16 the falsification test against database+LLM) across twelve question groups (What is Knowledge, Knowledge as mathematical object, measure theory, Knowledge Space, time/change, Knowledge identity, the computer brain's operations, KnowledgeOS, the Kernel, OS-analogy, the observation-to-action cycle), with an explicit research-discipline register (FACT/MATHEMATICAL RESULT/EXTERNAL RESEARCH RESULT/INTERPRETATION/HYPOTHESIS/MODEL/ARCHITECTURAL CONSEQUENCE/IMPLEMENTATION CONSEQUENCE) and four required final deliverables (definitions of Knowledge, Knowledge Space, KnowledgeOS, KnowledgeOS Kernel).

A response to the brain-of-a-computer research programme concluding Knowledge is probably not the Kernel's fundamental object; the fundamental object may instead be the epistemic history from which different forms of Knowledge can be reconstructed and evaluated. Proposes the Kernel sits below/before Knowledge Space (pre-space historical substrate feeding multiple constructed representations -- epistemic model, knowledge space, logical model), draws on Doignon and Falmagne's Knowledge Space Theory (Q,𝒦) as an existing, distinct mathematical meaning of 'Knowledge Space' requiring disambiguation from KnowledgeOS's broader sense, on W3C PROV for multi-version entity representation, and on seL4/microkernel minimal-trusted-computing-base principles for a sharper Kernel test (Remove(X) => a fundamental guarantee fails, rather than X is useful => X in Kernel); narrows Kernel candidates to Identity+History+Provenance+Context+Temporal-Integrity+Reconstruction, smaller than the earlier 10-12-object models.
